why_how.text: Signs and the people who direct traffic tell you what the road ahead requires, often before you can see it.
Warning signs give you time to slow down or change lanes before a hazard arrives.

scenario.text: At a busy corner, a crossing guard signals Dan to stop even though his light is green.

reasoning.text: A person directing traffic must be obeyed even when a light or sign says something different.

result.text: Dan stops and waits for the guard to wave him on.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a green light outranks a crossing guard's signal.

correction.text: You must obey a police officer, crossing guard or other worker directing traffic, even if the light or sign differs.

prompt.text: A worker holding a sign tells you to stop, but the traffic light ahead is green. What do you do?

answer.text: Stop and follow the worker's direction.

rationale.text: A person directing traffic outranks the light or sign, so you obey the worker.

narration.text: Welcome to the signs chapter. Road signs are the road's way of talking to you, and the separate highway signs test checks how well you understand them. This first lesson starts with a rule that sits above every sign: when a police officer, school crossing guard or other worker is directing traffic, you follow that person. Then it introduces the warning sign family, the yellow signs that alert you to hazards ahead, and walks through the first group of them: intersections, divided highways, slippery roads, signals, deer and lanes that end.

lines.text: Obey them over lights and signs.

narration.text: Police officers, school crossing guards and other workers sometimes direct traffic using signs. When they do, you must follow their directions even if they are different from the traffic light or sign on the road. A crossing guard may stop you at a green light so children can cross. In moments like that, the person's direction is the one that counts. Watch for their hand signals and signs as you approach, slow down, and be ready to stop wherever they tell you. Here is the trap: drivers who see a green light sometimes ignore the person in the road. A signal from an officer, guard or worker always comes first, even over a green light.

lines.text: Yellow with black words or symbols.

narration.text: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols, and most are diamond shaped. They tell you about a special situation or a hazard ahead, so their job is to buy you time. An Intersection or Cross Road sign marks a place ahead where two or more roads cross. A Divided Highway sign means the opposing lanes ahead will be separated by a physical barrier such as a guardrail. When you see any yellow diamond, ask what is coming and whether you need to slow down, change lanes or look harder for other traffic. Yellow is the color to remember.

lines.text: Signal Ahead: be ready to stop.

narration.text: Several warning signs ask you to slow down or get ready. A Slippery When Wet sign means the road ahead might be slippery, so slow down. A Signal Ahead sign warns that stop lights are ahead, so be ready to slow down and stop. A Deer Crossing sign marks an area where deer are very likely to cross the road, so stay alert, especially when visibility is poor. A Lane Ends sign shows which lane is ending; move into the other lane when it is safe, rather than racing to the end and forcing your way in at the last moment. Each one asks for a small, early adjustment.

lines.text: Worker says stop, light is green?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a worker holding a sign tells you to stop, but the traffic light ahead is green. What do you do? Remember the rule that sits above the signs. You stop and follow the worker's direction. A police officer, school crossing guard or other worker directing traffic outranks the light or sign, so their instruction is the one to follow, even when it seems to contradict the signal. When the worker waves you on, check the intersection again before you go, because other drivers may still be following the worker's earlier signals.

To wrap up: people directing traffic, such as police officers, school crossing guards and other workers, must be obeyed even when a light or sign says something different. Warning signs are yellow with black words or symbols, mostly diamond shaped, and alert you to hazards ahead. Intersection signs mark crossing roads, Divided Highway signs mean a barrier is coming, Slippery When Wet and Signal Ahead mean slow down and be ready, Deer Crossing means stay alert, and Lane Ends means move over when safe. Next come more warning signs.

why_how.text: Curves, hills and merging lanes change how you need to drive, and warning signs show them in advance.
Crossing signs warn you where pedestrians and children may be on the road.

scenario.text: Kim sees a Merge sign and assumes her own lane is ending.

reasoning.text: A Merge sign shows a lane joining, while a Lane Ends sign shows your own lane ending.

result.text: Kim stays in her lane and watches for the joining traffic, moving over only if it is safe and needed.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a Curved Road sign and a Sharp Turn sign as the same warning.

correction.text: A Sharp Turn sign means be ready to slow for the turn, while a Curved Road sign marks a gradual bend.

memory_support.text: Gentle curve ease off; sharp turn slow more.

prompt.text: You see a pedestrian symbol with an arrow plaque below it. What must you do?

answer.text: Yield to anyone crossing where the arrow shows.

rationale.text: The arrow plaque shows where the crossing is, and drivers must yield to crossing pedestrians.

narration.text: This lesson continues the yellow warning family. You will learn the signs for curved roads and sharp turns, merging lanes and hills, the sign that marks where a one-way road becomes two-way, and the Stop Ahead and Roundabout Ahead signs. Then the lesson covers the crossing signs that protect people on foot: pedestrian crossings and school zones and crossings. Several of these look alike at a glance, so the lesson points out the small differences in meaning that test questions often focus on, such as a gradual curve versus a sharp turn.

lines.text: Sharp Turn: be ready to slow.

narration.text: A Curved Road sign warns that the road bends gradually right or left, and you slow down only as much as needed to drive it safely. A Sharp Turn sign can show a left or right arrow and asks you to be ready to slow down when turning on that road; it is a stronger warning than the gradual Curved Road sign. A Hill sign warns of a hill ahead, and you slow down if needed to stay safe. With all three, the idea is to adjust your speed before the curve, turn or hill, not while you are already in it. Slow before the bend, not in it.

A Merge sign can show a right or left lane merge; make sure to move over to the next lane when it is safe to do so, and watch for vehicles joining. A Lane Ends sign is different: it shows your own lane ending. A Two-Way Traffic sign appears where you are leaving a one-way roadway and entering a road with opposing traffic, so expect oncoming vehicles from that point on. These signs all describe a change in how lanes are arranged ahead, so read them early and plan your lane position before the change. Plan your lane before the change arrives.

lines.text: Stop Ahead: arrow over a stop shape.

narration.text: A Stop Ahead sign warns of a stop sign ahead; it shows an arrow with the shape of a stop sign below it, and you slow down so you can stop safely. Begin slowing as soon as you see it. A Roundabout Ahead sign is a diamond containing a counterclockwise symbol, with a rectangular plaque below reading Roundabout Ahead. When you see it, slow down and start looking for the lane signs and yield signs that tell you how to enter the roundabout safely, as you learned in the right-of-way lessons. Both signs warn you to prepare before you arrive, so ease off the gas early.

lines.text: School signs: fluorescent green or yellow.

narration.text: A Pedestrian Crossing sign shows a pedestrian in the main diamond and an arrow in the rectangular sign below, which shows where the crossing is. Yield to crossing pedestrians. School crossing and school zone signs show pedestrians with an arrow below, may be fluorescent green or yellow, and are specific to school zones and crossings; there too, you yield to crossing pedestrians. The bright fluorescent color is meant to catch your eye, so treat it as an instant cue to slow down and scan both sides of the road for children.

lines.text: Lane Ends: your lane is ending.

narration.text: Here is the trap: two signs about lanes that sound alike. A Merge sign shows a lane joining from the right or left, while a Lane Ends sign shows your own lane ending. In both cases you move over when it is safe, but the reason differs. With a merge, other traffic is coming into the road, so you watch for it and make room. With lane ends, you are the one who must leave your lane. A question that asks which sign means your lane is ending is looking for Lane Ends, not Merge. Read the picture carefully before you act, because the right response depends on whose lane is affected.

lines.text: Walker symbol with an arrow plaque?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you see a pedestrian symbol with an arrow plaque below it. What must you do? Think about what the arrow tells you. You yield to anyone crossing where the arrow shows. The arrow plaque marks where the crossing is, and drivers must yield to crossing pedestrians. The same duty applies at school zones and school crossings, whose signs may be fluorescent green or yellow. Slow down as you approach, scan both sides of the road, and be ready to stop well before the crossing if anyone is waiting. Yielding there is always required.

lines.text: Yield at pedestrian and school crossings.

narration.text: In summary: a Curved Road sign marks a gradual bend, while a Sharp Turn sign means be ready to slow more. A Hill sign means slow if needed. A Merge sign shows a lane joining, unlike Lane Ends, where your lane stops. Two-Way Traffic marks where a one-way road meets opposing traffic. Stop Ahead warns of a stop sign ahead, and Roundabout Ahead is a diamond with a counterclockwise symbol. At pedestrian and school crossings, yield to people crossing. Next you will move from warnings to regulatory signs, the signs that state the rules.

why_how.text: Regulatory signs state rules you must obey, so knowing them keeps you legal.
Speed-related signs adjust your speed for the road and for children nearby.
Turn prohibitions and island signs keep drivers out of illegal or dangerous moves.

scenario.text: Eva sees a Reduced Speed Ahead sign and keeps her speed because the road looks clear.

reasoning.text: Reduced Speed Ahead is a regulatory sign telling her to slow down for conditions ahead.

result.text: Eva slows down before reaching the lower limit.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking Reduced Speed Ahead is just a warning like Slippery When Wet.

correction.text: Slippery When Wet is a yellow warning sign, but Reduced Speed Ahead is a regulatory sign telling you to slow down.

memory_support.text: Yellow warns, white and red rule.

prompt.text: A white sign shows a turn arrow with a slash through it. What does it tell you?

answer.text: You may not turn in the direction the arrow points.

rationale.text: A No Turn sign points toward the direction you may not turn, while a No U-turn sign forbids turning around.

narration.text: This lesson covers regulatory signs, the signs that tell you the rules of the road. Unlike warning signs, which alert you to hazards, regulatory signs tell you what you must or must not do. You will learn their shapes and colors, and then several common examples: Do Not Enter, Speed Limit, Reduced Speed Ahead, the school zone speed limit, Keep Right, and the signs that forbid turning or turning around. The lesson also clears up one family mix-up that often appears on the signs test, about which speed-related sign is a warning and which is a rule.

lines.text: Black, red, white or green letters.

narration.text: Regulatory signs are square, rectangular or a special shape. They can be white or red with black, red, white or green lettering and symbols, and they tell you the rules of the road. The special shapes, such as the octagon and the downward triangle, are reserved for the most important rules and are covered in the next lesson. For now, remember the basic contrast: yellow means a warning, while white or red usually means a rule you must obey. Knowing the color code lets you recognize a sign's family even before you can read its words.

lines.text: Do Not Enter: you may not go in.
Speed Limit: maximum in good conditions.

narration.text: A Do Not Enter sign means you cannot enter. It is used on exit ramps going the wrong direction and on one-way streets, so seeing it from the driver's seat means you are about to go the wrong way. A Speed Limit sign indicates the maximum speed you can drive in good driving conditions; in bad conditions, a lower speed may be needed. A Reduced Speed Ahead sign means you should slow down, for example because a slippery road may lie ahead. Begin slowing as soon as you see it, so you reach the lower speed before the new limit begins.

lines.text: School speed: when children are visible.
Keep Right: island or obstacle ahead.

narration.text: On a school zone speed limit sign, you cannot go over the posted speed when children are visible. A Keep Right sign means a traffic island or obstacle divides the road ahead, so stay to its right. A No Turn sign points in the direction you are not allowed to turn, and a No U-turn sign means you cannot make a U-turn. These signs are often placed at intersections and medians, so watch for them before choosing your lane. Turning against one of them is a violation even when no other traffic is around. Watch for these at medians and corners.

Here is the trap: two signs that both make you think about slowing down. Slippery When Wet is a yellow warning about the road surface, while Reduced Speed Ahead is a regulatory sign telling you to lower your speed. One describes a hazard and lets you judge how much to slow; the other states a rule that the speed is about to drop. On the signs test, a question may show one and ask which family it belongs to. Use the color and the wording: yellow and descriptive means warning; white and instructive means rule. The family decides how strictly to respond.

Here is a quick check: a white sign shows a turn arrow with a slash through it. What does it tell you? Think about the No Turn sign. You may not turn in the direction the arrow points. A No Turn sign points toward the direction you may not turn, while a No U-turn sign forbids turning around. Both are regulatory signs, so they are rules, not suggestions. If you need to go that way, continue to the next intersection where the turn is allowed, rather than making the forbidden turn because the road looks empty. Rules apply even on empty roads.

lines.text: White or red signs state rules.

narration.text: To sum up: regulatory signs state the rules; they are square, rectangular or a special shape, white or red with black, red, white or green lettering. Do Not Enter means you may not go in and is used on wrong-way ramps and one-way streets. A Speed Limit sign gives the maximum in good conditions, and Reduced Speed Ahead tells you to slow down. A school zone limit may not be exceeded when children are visible. Keep Right means an island divides the road, and No Turn and No U-turn forbid those moves. Next come lane-use signs and the key shapes.

why_how.text: Lane-use signs at roundabouts tell you which lane to be in before you enter.
A few shapes, the octagon, the downward triangle, the orange triangle and the pennant, carry critical rules.

scenario.text: Tom wants to turn left at a two-lane roundabout and lines up in the right lane.

reasoning.text: In the two-lane example, only the left lane is for turning left or making a U-turn.

result.text: Tom moves to the left lane before entering.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a Yield sign requires the same full stop as a Stop sign.

correction.text: A Stop sign requires a complete stop, while a Yield sign requires giving the right-of-way to other vehicles.

memory_support.text: Eight sides stop, triangle yields, pennant no passing.

prompt.text: You see an orange triangle with reflective markings on the back of a tractor ahead. What does it tell you?

answer.text: The vehicle may be traveling at twenty-five miles per hour or less.

rationale.text: The orange triangle is the Slow Moving Vehicle emblem, which is different from the yellow no passing pennant.

lines.text: Stop, yield, slow vehicles, no passing.

narration.text: This lesson has two parts. First you will learn to read roundabout lane-use signs, which use arrows and lines to show which lane goes where; the handbook gives three examples, and each one assigns the lanes differently. Then you will learn the key regulatory shapes that matter most on the road: the eight-sided Stop sign, the downward Yield triangle, the orange Slow Moving Vehicle emblem and the yellow No Passing Zone pennant, plus the rule for reserved parking spaces. Shapes are especially important because you can recognize them even when the words are hard to read.

On a roundabout lane-use sign, the dot on the left-turn arrow stands for the center of the roundabout, and the lines on the sign show the different lanes. In the two-lane example, you can only use the left lane to turn left or make a U-turn, and you use the right lane to go straight or turn right. The sign is posted before the roundabout so you can choose your lane in time. Read it as a map of the lanes in front of you: each arrow belongs to the lane below it, and you pick the lane whose arrows include your direction. Pick the lane that matches your move.

The handbook gives two more examples. In the three-lane example, the far-left lane is used to go left or stay straight, the middle lane is to go straight, and the right lane is to turn right. In another two-lane example, the far-left lane is used only to turn left, while the right lane may turn left or go straight. Notice that the two-lane examples do not match each other. That is the lesson: never assume which lane turns where. Every roundabout can set its lanes differently, so read the arrows on the sign each time you approach.

lines.text: Stop: eight sides, red, full stop.
Yield: red and white, pointing down.

narration.text: A Stop sign has eight sides and is red with white letters. You must come to a complete stop and wait until your path is clear before continuing. A Yield sign is a downward pointing red and white triangle with red letters, and it means you must yield the right-of-way to other vehicles. Learn the shapes well, because the shape tells you the rule even before you can read the words. When you see either one, get ready to brake. At a Stop sign, the full stop comes first and the decision to go comes after; at a Yield sign, slow down and be ready to stop if another vehicle has the right-of-way.

Here is the trap. Both signs are red and white, and both are about letting others go first, so learners blur them. A Stop sign is red with white letters and eight sides and requires a complete stop. A Yield sign is a downward red and white triangle that requires giving the right-of-way to other vehicles. Rolling through a stop sign because the road looks clear is a violation, while at a yield sign the key duty is to let other vehicles go first. Match the shape to the action: octagon means stop, downward triangle means yield. Shape first, then action.

lines.text: Reserved parking: permit or plate only.

narration.text: A Slow Moving Vehicle emblem is a triangle-shaped sign with reflective orange markings, and the vehicle carrying it could be traveling at twenty-five miles per hour or less. When you spot one ahead, slow down early and keep a safe distance. A No Passing Zone sign is a yellow pennant with black lettering, and you are not allowed to pass any vehicle in the no passing zone. Before you pull out to pass, look for the pennant, and if you see it, stay in your lane until the zone ends. One more regulatory sign: a reserved parking space may be used only with a valid disabled parking permit or plate.

Here is a quick check: you see an orange triangle with reflective markings on the back of a tractor ahead. What does it tell you? Recall the special shapes. The vehicle may be traveling at twenty-five miles per hour or less. The orange triangle is the Slow Moving Vehicle emblem, which is different from the yellow No Passing Zone pennant. Slow down early, keep a safe distance, and pass only where passing is allowed and you have enough room ahead, never inside a zone marked with the yellow pennant. Patience behind slow vehicles is part of safe driving.

In summary: on a roundabout lane-use sign the dot marks the center and the lines mark the lanes, and the examples show that each roundabout can assign lanes differently, so always read the arrows. A Stop sign is an eight-sided red sign requiring a complete stop, and a Yield sign is a downward red and white triangle requiring you to give the right-of-way. The orange Slow Moving Vehicle triangle marks a vehicle that may go twenty-five miles per hour or less, the yellow pennant marks a no passing zone, and reserved spaces need a disabled permit or plate.

why_how.text: Work zones put people on or near the road, so their signs and rules protect workers and drivers.
Work zones carry special penalties and phone rules.
Flaggers control traffic in person, so their directions come first.

scenario.text: Lucas enters a work zone and picks up his phone to text that he will be late.

reasoning.text: In a construction zone you may use a cellphone only to report an emergency, and fines are doubled there.

result.text: Lucas waits until he is out of the zone and parked safely.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking orange signs are just another kind of yellow warning.

correction.text: Yellow signs warn of road hazards in general, while orange signs warn that people are working on or near the road.

memory_support.text: Orange means workers: slow down, fines double.

prompt.text: A worker holding a flag signals you to stop in a work zone. What must you do?

answer.text: Stop and follow the flagger's directions.

rationale.text: A flagger's directions must be followed, while a Road Workers Ahead sign only asks you to slow down or move over.

narration.text: This lesson covers construction, maintenance and emergency work zones. You will learn how to recognize work zone signs by their color, what to do when you see orange signs, cones and flags, and two special rules that apply in construction zones: doubled fines and a strict limit on phone use. Then the lesson covers the people and signs you will meet in a work zone, from flaggers to road work signs that tell you how far away the work is. Work zones change often, so these rules are about staying alert and slowing down every time.

lines.text: Warn of workers on or near the road.

narration.text: Construction signs are for construction, maintenance or emergency workers. They are an orange diamond or rectangle with black lettering and symbols, and they warn you about people working on or near the road. You will often see orange signs, cones and flags around these work areas, and that is your signal to slow down. The orange color stands out from the yellow of ordinary warning signs on purpose: it tells you that the hazard ahead includes people, not just a road condition, and people on foot near moving traffic need extra space and lower speeds.

lines.text: Traffic fines double in work zones.
Phone only to report an emergency.

narration.text: Traffic fines double in construction work areas, so a speeding ticket in a work zone costs twice as much. You can only use your cellphone in a construction zone if you are reporting an emergency. That means no calls, texts or browsing while you drive through, even in slow traffic. Both rules exist because work zones combine narrow lanes, sudden stops and workers close to traffic. A moment of distraction there is far more likely to hurt someone, so keep both hands on the wheel and your eyes on the lane until you reach the end of the zone.

lines.text: Road Workers Ahead: slow or move over.
Road Work Ahead: shows the distance.

narration.text: A Road Construction Flagger Ahead sign warns of a worker with a sign or a flag, and you must follow their directions. A Road Workers Ahead sign means road workers are up ahead, so slow down or move over. A Road Work Ahead sign tells you how far ahead the construction work is, and again you slow down or move over. The distance on that sign changes from site to site, so read it each time; it tells you how much time you have to adjust your speed and lane before you reach the workers and their equipment. Each sign tells you how to adjust.

lines.text: Orange: people working near the road.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Yellow and orange diamonds look alike from a distance, so drivers treat them the same. They are not the same. Yellow signs warn of road hazards in general, while orange signs warn that people are working on or near the road. Orange also brings the special work zone rules: doubled fines and no phone use except to report an emergency. On the signs test, a question may describe a sign's color and ask what it means. If it is orange, think workers, slow down, and remember the stricter rules that come with it.

Here is a quick check: a worker holding a flag signals you to stop in a work zone. What must you do? Think about the difference between people and signs in a work zone. You stop and follow the flagger's directions. A flagger's directions must be followed, while a Road Workers Ahead sign only asks you to slow down or move over. Watch the flagger for the signal to proceed, then drive through slowly, keep your phone down unless you are reporting an emergency, and remember that any fine there would be doubled. Calm, slow driving keeps workers safe.

To finish: construction signs are orange diamonds or rectangles with black letters that warn of construction, maintenance or emergency workers. Orange signs, cones and flags mean slow down. Traffic fines double in work zones, and you may use a cellphone there only to report an emergency. Follow a flagger's directions, and slow down or move over at Road Workers Ahead and Road Work Ahead signs, which tell you how far away the work is. Next you will learn the guide signs that help you find your way: destination, service and mile marker signs.

why_how.text: Guide signs help you find your way and your exit without sudden moves.
Service signs and mile markers help you find help and tell others where you are.

scenario.text: Nia needs a hospital and is watching the green signs for directions.

reasoning.text: Blue service signs point to services such as a hospital, while green and brown signs point to destinations.

result.text: Nia follows the blue hospital sign.

claim.text: Common mistake: looking for a hospital on the green destination signs.

correction.text: Hospitals and other services are shown on blue service signs, not on green or brown destination signs.

memory_support.text: Green and brown go places; blue finds services.

prompt.text: You need to tell a dispatcher where you are on a highway. Which sign helps most?

answer.text: A mile marker, which shows the direction, route number and mile number.

rationale.text: Mile markers show where you are on the road and help emergency crews reach highway incidents faster.

narration.text: This lesson covers the signs that help you find your way. You will learn the green and brown destination signs, exit and roundabout exit signs, and street name signs. Then you will learn the blue service signs that point to things like camping and hospitals, and the mile markers that tell you exactly where you are on a highway. Guide signs do not give orders the way regulatory signs do, but reading them early lets you choose your lane and exit calmly instead of making a last-second move that surprises other drivers. Read them early.

lines.text: Brown for fun or scenic places.

narration.text: Destination signs are square or rectangular, green or brown with white lettering. They show directions and distances to different places, such as cities, states and airports, and they can also show you how to get to parks, historical areas or museums. Brown destination signs show information about fun or beautiful places, and some show how many miles it will take you to get there. So green and brown guide signs both give directions, but brown ones point to recreational or scenic places, while green ones cover cities, highways and general destinations.

lines.text: Exit arrow shows the exit's side.

narration.text: Exit signs tell you which way the exit is, and the arrow shows which side of the road the exit is located on, so you know which lane to move into. Roundabout exit signs show you which road you will be on when you exit the roundabout at each exit. Street name signs tell you the name of the road; they are located on almost every corner, posted on top of a silver pole facing the road they are named after. Reading these early gives you time to signal and change lanes smoothly before your turn or exit arrives. Early reading means smooth lane changes.

lines.text: Blue with white letters or symbols.

narration.text: Service signs are square or rectangular and blue with white letters or symbols. They show you how to get to different services nearby, such as camping or a hospital, and some show where there is access for the disabled. The blue color is the clue: when you need fuel, food, lodging or medical help, look for blue signs rather than the green destination signs. A hospital sign with an arrow, for example, shows which direction the hospital is located, which can save precious time in an emergency on an unfamiliar road. Look for blue when you need help.

lines.text: Every one to two-tenths of a mile.

narration.text: Mile markers, also known as reference markers, are tall, thin rectangular blue or green signs with white lettering. They help you locate where you are on the road and improve emergency response times to highway incidents. Each mile marker includes the direction of travel, the route number and the mile number, and they are placed every one to two-tenths of a mile on the right side of the road or in the median. If you ever need to report a crash or a breakdown, reading the nearest marker tells responders exactly where to find you.

Here is the trap. Guide signs come in three colors, and learners mix up their jobs. Blue signs point to services such as a hospital or camping, while green and brown signs point to destinations. Brown is the special case for fun or scenic places such as parks. Mile markers add one more wrinkle: they can be blue or green, but you recognize them by their tall, thin shape and the direction, route and mile number they carry. So when you sort a guide sign, look at color first and then at shape before deciding what it is telling you.

lines.text: Need to tell a dispatcher where you are?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you need to tell a dispatcher where you are on a highway. Which sign helps most? Think about which sign carries exact location numbers. A mile marker, which shows the direction of travel, the route number and the mile number. Mile markers show where you are on the road and help emergency crews reach highway incidents faster. They appear every one to two-tenths of a mile on the right side or in the median, so one is usually close by; read the nearest one and pass all three pieces to the dispatcher. Accurate location speeds up help.

To wrap up: destination signs are green or brown with white letters and show directions and distances, with brown for fun or scenic places. An Exit sign's arrow shows which side the exit is on, roundabout exit signs show the road at each exit, and street name signs sit on silver poles on almost every corner. Blue service signs point to services like camping and hospitals. Mile markers are tall, thin blue or green signs showing direction, route and mile number every one to two-tenths of a mile. Next you will learn the route number signs.

why_how.text: Route markers tell you what kind of road you are on and help you follow a route.
Each road type has its own marker shape, so the shape alone tells you a lot.

scenario.text: Ivan's directions say to follow a state road, and he sees a white sign shaped like a police badge.

reasoning.text: A police badge shape marks a U.S. route; a state road marker looks like a milk jug.

result.text: Ivan keeps going until he finds the milk jug marker for his state road.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking all route markers look the same.

correction.text: Route number signs change shape and color depending on the type of road.

memory_support.text: Shield interstate, badge U.S., jug state, rectangle county.

prompt.text: You see a white route marker with rounded edges shaped like a rectangle. What kind of road is it?

rationale.text: County roads use a white rounded rectangle, while state roads use the milk jug shape.

narration.text: This short lesson is about route number signs. Their shape and color change depending on the type of road you are traveling on, and they help you navigate the routes to your destination. You will learn four markers: the Interstate shield, the U.S. route badge, the state road milk jug and the county road rectangle. Because route markers are often small and far away, recognizing the shape is quicker than reading the words, and it helps you confirm that you are still on the right road after turns, merges and interchanges. Shape is the quickest clue.

The Interstate Highway sign looks like a shield with red on top and blue on the bottom, and it has white lettering. The U.S. Route sign looks like a police badge; it is normally grey or white with black lettering, and these roads form a network of roads and highways across the United States. So the two federal markers differ clearly in color: the interstate shield is red and blue, while the U.S. route badge is grey or white. When directions mention an interstate, look for the colored shield, not the plain badge. Color separates the two.

The state road sign looks like a milk jug with a spout at the bottom, and it is white with black lettering. The county road sign is rectangular with rounded edges, and it is also white with black lettering. Because both are white with black letters, the shape is what tells them apart: the milk jug means a state road, while the rounded rectangle means a county road. Knowing this helps when your directions name a state highway and you need to be sure you have not turned onto a county road with a similar number. Shape separates the two.

Here is a bridge to tie the four markers together. Route number signs change shape and color with the type of road. A U.S. route sign looks like a police badge and is usually grey or white with black letters, unlike the red and blue interstate shield. A state road sign is shaped like a milk jug with its spout at the bottom, while a county road sign is a white rectangle with rounded edges. If you remember one shape per road type, shield, badge, jug and rectangle, you can name the road type from the marker even before you can read its number.

Here is a quick check: you see a white route marker shaped like a rectangle with rounded edges. What kind of road is it? Run through the four shapes. It is a county road. County roads use a white rounded rectangle, while state roads use the milk jug shape, U.S. routes use the police badge, and interstates use the red and blue shield. Both county and state markers are white with black letters, which is exactly why the shape is the deciding clue when you are trying to confirm which road you are on. Shape is the deciding clue every time.

lines.text: Shape and color show the road type.

narration.text: To sum up: route number signs change shape and color with the type of road and help you follow a route. The Interstate sign is a shield, red on top and blue on the bottom, with white lettering. A U.S. route sign looks like a police badge, usually grey or white with black lettering. A state road sign is shaped like a milk jug with the spout at the bottom, and a county road sign is a white rectangle with rounded edges, both with black lettering. Next you will learn the railroad crossing signs and rules, the last part of the signs chapter.

why_how.text: Trains cannot stop quickly or swerve, so crossing rules and signs exist to keep you off the tracks when one is coming.
Each railroad sign and device tells you something specific about the crossing ahead.

scenario.text: At a two-track crossing, a freight train passes and Rosa starts across as soon as the last car clears.

reasoning.text: With two sets of tracks, wait until the train is far enough away to see the other tracks are clear.

result.text: Rosa waits until she can see the second track is clear, then crosses.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a crossing has only one track if no number-of-tracks sign is posted.

correction.text: Not all crossings with more than one track post the sign, so always check for additional tracks before crossing.

memory_support.text: Never race, never stop on, never go around.

prompt.text: The crossing lights stop flashing as a train clears, but the bell is still ringing. May you go?

answer.text: No. Wait until the bell or horn has stopped.

rationale.text: Where a crossing has a bell or horn with its lights, do not cross until the sound has stopped and the track is clear.

narration.text: This final lesson of the signs chapter covers railroad crossings. You will learn the basic safety rules that apply at every crossing, the different railroad signs and what each one tells you, special plaques you may see, the blue emergency sign, the danger of multiple tracks, and the gates, lights, bells and horns that warn of an approaching train. The handbook reminds us that trains are large, heavy and moving faster than they seem, which is why these rules leave no room for guessing. Learning them well could save your life.

lines.text: Room on the far side before crossing.

narration.text: Never try to race a train across the tracks. Do not stop on the tracks, and do not cross the tracks if there is not room for your vehicle on the other side; traffic backed up beyond the crossing can leave you trapped on the rails. Do not shift gears while crossing the railroad tracks. Before you cross, make sure to look both ways, even if the railroad signals are not flashing, because signals can fail. Remember that trains are big and heavy and travel faster than they appear to, so a train that looks far away may reach you very quickly.

lines.text: Round yellow sign with an X.

narration.text: The railroad advance warning sign is round with a yellow background and an X symbol with black lettering; it tells you there is a railroad crossing ahead, so be alert and watch for a train. At the crossing, a crossbuck with flashing lights warns when a train is coming: the lights flash when a train approaches from either direction, and you wait until they stop and the track is clear. A white X-shaped crossbuck with a Yield sign posted below it means you must yield to trains that are crossing. Each sign is a step closer to the tracks.

lines.text: White crossbuck: at the crossing, lists tracks.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Both signs use an X, so people mix them up. The round yellow railroad warning sign with an X tells you a crossing is there ahead of you, while the white X-shaped crossbuck stands at the crossing itself and also lists how many tracks you will cross. Two special plaques add meaning. A Tracks out-of-service sign means the tracks are no longer used, while an Exempt sign means only certain vehicles are excused from stopping before crossing. Neither plaque is a reason to skip looking both ways. Look both ways every time, plaque or not.

lines.text: Blue sign with a phone number.
Not every multi-track crossing is marked.
Wait until all tracks are clear.

narration.text: A blue Report Problem or Emergency sign with white letters stands at every highway-railroad crossing and lists a phone number to report unsafe conditions, such as a vehicle stuck on the tracks or a warning light that is not working. Crossings with more than one track often post a sign showing the number of tracks, but not all do, so always check for more than one track before crossing. When there are two sets of tracks, wait until the train is far enough away that you can see the other tracks are clear, before you start across.

lines.text: Gate down: a train is coming.
Never drive around or under it.
Wait for bells and horns to stop.

narration.text: A railroad gate lowers when a train is coming. Do not drive around the gate or under a gate that is rising or lowering; gates are there because a train is close, and squeezing past one is one of the most dangerous choices a driver can make. Some crossings also have a bell or horn along with the lights. Do not cross until the bell or horn has stopped. Treat every one of these devices the same way: as long as a gate is moving, lights are flashing, or a bell or horn is sounding, you stay stopped behind the crossing. Patience at the crossing is always the right choice.

Here is a quick check: the crossing lights stop flashing as a train clears, but the bell is still ringing. May you go? Think about each warning device. The answer is no. Wait until the bell or horn has stopped. Where a crossing has a bell or horn with its lights, do not cross until the sound has stopped and the track is clear. If there is a second set of tracks, also wait until you can see that those tracks are clear, and never drive around a gate that is still moving up or down. Every warning device must be silent and still before you cross, and you should still look both ways.

lines.text: Never race, stop on or squeeze across.
Wait for lights, gates and bells.

narration.text: To finish the signs chapter: never race a train, never stop on the tracks, and do not cross without room beyond. Do not change gears on the tracks, and look both ways even when lights are not flashing, because trains are faster than they seem. The round yellow sign warns of a crossing ahead; a crossbuck with lights means wait until they stop; a crossbuck with a Yield sign means yield to trains. Check for multiple tracks, use the blue sign's number to report problems, never drive around a gate, and wait until bells and horns stop.
